item.title: Don't Build AI Apps From Scratch. Use This Free Repo Instead
item.description:
Before you build your next AI app from zero, check whether someone has already built it. There’s a good chance they have, and that the code is sitting in one GitHub repo.

Awesome LLM Apps by Shubham Saboo has more than a hundred working AI apps in a single repository: agents, voice assistants, agent teams, generative UI, MCP agents and more. It has over 144,000 stars and it’s completely free. In the video I go through every section and then run one app on my own computer. This post covers the same ground in written form, with every command you need.

🎥 Watch the Video

👉 Watch on YouTube: Don’t Build AI Apps From Scratch

What Awesome LLM Apps Is

Many “awesome” repos on GitHub are just lists of links. This one is different: every app lives inside the repo. You open a folder and the code is right there.

  • License: Apache 2.0. You can clone it, change it, use it in your own projects and even build a product on top of it.
  • Models: it isn’t locked to one AI company. Apps use Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Llama, Qwen and other open models.
  • Local options: some apps run fully on your own machine with Ollama, with no API key at all.

🔗 Repo: github.com/Shubhamsaboo/awesome-llm-apps

The README splits everything into 16 sections. Here’s what’s in each one.

Agent Skills

These aren’t browser apps. They’re skills you add to a coding agent like Claude Code, Cursor or Codex, and then use in plain English.

  • Project Graveyard finds the side projects you’ve abandoned, explains why each one died, and helps you finish the one worth going back to.
  • First Reader simulates real readers going through your draft and tells you where they get bored or stop, without rewriting a word.
  • Scope Creep Detector checks whether a code change grew bigger than it was meant to be.
  • Commit Archaeologist digs through Git history to explain why a piece of code exists.
  • Dependency Doctor flags old, broken or risky packages in your dependency file.
  • Thinking Out Loud turns a messy voice ramble into a clean, short brief.
  • Self-Improving Agent Skills is a project where skills test themselves and get better automatically.

Standalone Apps and Tools

  • Excaliflow: hand-drawn system diagrams with animated arrows, exportable as video.
  • Needle: a Chrome extension that searches a page by meaning, not exact words.
  • Ripple: watches a Google Doc and finds what else must change when you edit one thing.

Starter AI Agents

If you’re new to agents, start here. They’re small and easy to read.

Agent What it does
Blog to Podcast Turns any blog link into a narrated podcast episode
Data Analysis Answers plain-English questions about a CSV or Excel file
Travel Agent Builds a day-by-day trip plan, with local and cloud versions
Music Generator Turns a prompt into an MP3 track
Meme Generator Makes memes by driving a real web browser
Medical Imaging Analyses X-rays and scans
Web Scraping Scrapes the data you describe
Mixture of Agents Asks several models, then combines the best answer
Breakup Recovery A team of agents that talks you through a breakup

Advanced AI Agents

Once you’re comfortable, this section gets serious:

  • Home Renovation Agent: photos of your room in, renovation plan and realistic images out.
  • Deep Research Agent: full web research and a written report on any topic.
  • System Architect Agent: reviews software architecture with a reasoning model plus Claude.
  • Investment Agent: compares stocks and builds a report from Yahoo Finance data.
  • Earnings Call Analyst: turns YouTube earnings calls into a synced analysis workspace.
  • Movie Production Agent: one-line idea in, script drafts and casting ideas out.
  • Journalist Agent: researches, writes and edits articles.
  • Health & Fitness Agent: diet and workout plans based on your goals.
  • Meeting Agent: context, industry insights and a strategy brief before a meeting.
  • Fraud Investigation Agent: cross-checks public records to flag inconsistencies.
  • Self-Evolving Agent: rewrites its own workflow to improve over time.

Always-on Agents

These run on a schedule instead of waiting for you to ask:

  • Hacker News Briefing Agent: a ranked daily brief sent to Slack or email.
  • Release Radar Agent: watches your dependencies for breaking changes, security fixes and major updates.

Multi-agent Teams

Instead of one AI doing everything, a team of agents each takes one job:

  • Finance Agent Team: a financial analyst team in about twenty lines of Python.
  • Legal Agent Team: research, contract analysis and strategy, with a local version too.
  • Recruitment Agent Team: from resume screening to interview scheduling.
  • Real Estate Agent Team: property search, market analysis and recommendations.
  • Teaching Agent Team: a complete learning path from a “faculty” of agents.
  • Game Design Agent Team: full game concepts from design specialists.
  • Multimodal Coding Agent Team: photo of a coding problem in, working solution out.
  • UI/UX Feedback Team: reviews your landing page and generates an improved version.
  • Competitor Intelligence Team: a competitor breakdown built from their own websites.
  • LLM Panel Team: three models review the same code change blind, then argue it out.

Voice AI Agents

  • Audio Tour Agent: a self-guided audio tour based on your location, interests and pace.
  • Customer Support Voice Agent: answers out loud using your own documents.
  • Insurance Claim Live Agent Team: takes your claim by voice, looks at the damage through your webcam and sketches what happened.
  • Voice dictation agent: an open-source agent that types wherever you talk.

Generative UI and Agentic Frontends

Here the AI builds the interface, not just the reply:

  • Dashboard Canvas Agent: describe a dashboard in chat and the charts appear on a live canvas.
  • Shadcn Component Generator: chat your way to ready-to-use UI components.
  • MCP App Builder: describe an app, get a live working version.
  • Financial Coach: your budget and savings plan as interactive cards.
  • Generative UI Starter: a kanban board you and the AI work on together.

Game-Playing Agents

  • Chess Agent: Agent White vs Agent Black, with every move validated.
  • Tic-Tac-Toe Agent: two different AI models play each other.
  • 3D PyGame Agent: writes game code and runs it live in the browser.

MCP AI Agents

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard way to connect AI to outside tools and data.

  • Browser MCP Agent: control a real browser by telling it what to do.
  • GitHub MCP Agent: explore any repo in plain English.
  • Notion MCP Agent: talk to your Notion pages from the terminal.
  • Travel Planner MCP Agent: trips built from live Airbnb and Google Maps data.
  • Dependency Upgrade Advisor: tells you what will break before you upgrade.

RAG, Memory and Chat with X

  • RAG: more than twenty apps that answer questions from your own documents, including fully local versions.
  • LLM Apps with Memory: apps that remember you, like a travel agent that learns your preferences and a local ChatGPT clone with per-user memory.
  • Chat with X: chat with your Gmail inbox, a PDF, a GitHub repo, YouTube videos, research papers or a Substack archive. Most are around thirty lines of code.

Optimization, Fine-tuning and Crash Courses

  • Optimization tools that cut the tokens you send, lowering your API bill.
  • Fine-tuning examples for small open models like Gemma and Llama, one of which runs free on Google Colab.
  • Crash courses for Google’s Agent Development Kit and the OpenAI Agents SDK.

Before You Run Any App

Open the app’s folder and read two files: the README and requirements.txt.

  • If you see “OpenAI API key” (or another provider’s key), you’ll pay for that model.
  • If you see Ollama, it usually runs locally on your own computer for free.

Demo: Run the Resume & Job Matcher Locally

I picked the Resume & Job Matcher from advanced_llm_apps/resume_job_matcher. You give it a resume PDF and a job description, and it returns a fit score out of 100, your strengths and what to improve. It runs on Ollama, so there’s no API key.

You need: Git, Python 3 and Ollama installed.

1. Download only this app

The repo is big, so use a sparse checkout to download just one folder:

1
2
3
4

git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Shubhamsaboo/awesome-llm-apps.git
cd awesome-llm-apps
git sparse-checkout set advanced_llm_apps/resume_job_matcher
cd advanced_llm_apps/resume_job_matcher

2. Create a virtual environment and install packages 

1
2
3
4

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate          # Windows
# source .venv/bin/activate     # macOS / Linux
pip install -r requirements.txt

3. Get the model

Open app.py. On line 68 the model is set to "llama3". Either pull that model, or change the word to a model you already have in Ollama:

1

ollama pull llama3

4. Start the app 

1

streamlit run app.py

The app opens in your browser. Upload the resume, paste or upload the job description, and in a few seconds you get a fit score, your strengths and what to improve for that exact job. Everything runs on your own computer: no account, no API key and no cost.

If you get an error

It’s almost always because Ollama isn’t running. Open the Ollama app, or run this in another terminal and try again:

1

ollama serve

Takeaways

Awesome LLM Apps is more than a hundred AI apps across sixteen sections, from simple starter agents to voice agents, agent teams and full crash courses. All of it is free and open source.

If you’re learning AI, don’t just read about it. Pick one app, run it, then change it and make it your own.

Which app are you trying first? Tell me in the comments on the video. Thanks for reading, and see you in the next one.

item.title: REA Tutorial: Reverse Engineer Any App with Claude Code (Setup, Fixes & Honest Review)
item.description:
There’s a GitHub repo called REA, Reverse Engineer Anything, and the hype around it is huge. People claim it can clone any software, and its star count has shot into the hundreds of thousands.

So I installed it, pointed it at a real app on my PC, and here’s my honest take: what it actually does, how to set it up (especially on Windows), the errors you’ll hit, and whether it’s worth it.

What REA Promises

REA makes three big promises:

  1. Inspect almost any software: desktop apps, Android apps, websites and even firmware.
  2. Explain how a feature works, not just what’s on screen, but what happens behind it.
  3. No source code needed. It works on apps already installed on your computer.

Why Everyone Is Talking About It

Give an AI a screenshot of an app and it can copy the look: layout, colours, buttons. That’s like judging a restaurant by its menu. You see the dishes, but you have no idea what’s happening in the kitchen.

REA lets the AI walk into the kitchen. It can check what happens when you click a button, where data is stored, which part of the app runs a feature, which servers it talks to, and how all the parts connect.

Separating Hype from Reality

What it really does:

  • Finds real evidence inside the app’s files
  • Explains that evidence in plain language
  • Tells you what it couldn’t figure out (my favourite part)

What it doesn’t do:

  • There’s no magic “clone this app” button. Your AI assistant still has to build and test things.
  • Heavily locked-down apps need extra tools and may still leave open questions.

Open, web-based apps reveal a lot. Heavily protected apps reveal much less.

How It Works: A Detective Story

Four pieces work together:

Piece Role In REA
Investigator Understands your question, decides what to look at Your AI agent (Claude Code, Codex…)
Playbook Training manual: what to check, how to follow clues, how to record doubts The REA skill
Connection Lets the agent call outside tools The MCP server
Scanners The actual analysis tools; REA picks the right one for each app 200+ REA analysis tools

The workflow is five steps: pick an app (or one feature), let REA inspect the installed files, collect evidence with proof for every finding, decide what to do with what you learned, then build and compare.

Confidence Labels

This is what makes REA different from an AI confidently guessing. Every finding is labelled:

  • Observed: seen directly in the app’s files
  • Derived: worked out from what it saw (2 + 2 = 4)
  • Inferred: a reasoned guess, and clearly marked as one
  • Unknown: couldn’t determine it, flagged for you to test

In my test, when REA checked VS Code’s security switches, it marked the result observed and attached the file’s fingerprint as proof.

Setup

You need Node.js 22.19 or newer. Check with:

1

node -v

Option A: Let Your Agent Install It

Copy the REA GitHub link into Claude Code and say “install this for me”. If anything fails, talk it through with the agent step by step.

Option B: The Setup Wizard 

1

npx rea-agents setup

The wizard asks which AI agent you use and connects REA to it.

The Windows Catch

On Windows, the wizard doesn’t update Claude Code’s settings for you, so you register REA yourself. These are the steps that worked for me:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

# 1. Install globally so the `rea` command works from any folder
npm install -g rea-agents

# 2. (Recommended) check that everything is in place
rea doctor

# 3. Register REA as an MCP server for Claude Code
claude mcp add rea -- cmd /c rea mcp

Then fully restart Claude Code and run /mcp to confirm REA is listed and connected.

The Real Test: What’s Inside VS Code?

Instead of a toy demo, I pointed REA at an app most of us use every day: VS Code. I opened Claude Code, pasted my prompt (it’s in the video description), approved the tool calls carefully, and waited. Here’s what came back.

What VS Code is made of. It’s built on Electron, a kit for building desktop apps with web technology. Inside is Chromium (the engine behind Chrome) plus Node.js, all packed into one large executable that’s officially signed by Microsoft. The giveaway is its internal name: electron.exe. VS Code is essentially a website running in its own private Chrome window.

Electron fuses. Electron apps have “fuses”, like the child lock on a car’s back door: set at the factory and hard to change later. REA showed which are on (for example, the one that lets code.exe act as a plain Node.js program, needed for the CLI and background helpers) and which are off. VS Code relies on its own checksum verification instead. These are design choices, not bugs, but it’s why security researchers love studying Electron apps.

Who VS Code talks to. Think of it as checking your phone’s call log: Microsoft’s update server (where “Restart to update” comes from), the extension marketplace, a GitHub-hosted gallery of MCP servers, A/B testing services, a Bing-backed settings search, and download servers for AI agents.

VS Code is a team, not one program. Like a restaurant kitchen:

  • The main process is the manager that starts everyone else.
  • The workbench window is the dining area, everything you see.
  • The shared process handles paperwork like installing extensions.
  • The extension host is a separate station where extensions run.
  • The PTY host runs your terminals, and a file watcher notices file changes.
  • A newer agent host runs AI agent sessions.

That explains something you’ve probably noticed: when one extension hangs, VS Code itself doesn’t freeze.

Errors I Hit and How to Fix Them

Error Fix
claude is not recognized as an internal or external command Add Claude Code’s bin folder to your PATH
MCP server rea already exists in user config Nothing to fix. Just restart Claude Code
/mcp doesn’t list REA Claude Code wasn’t fully restarted, or you’re in a different session. Close it completely and reopen it on the same PC
“Provider unavailable” REA is missing a provider for native .exe analysis. Install Ghidra and Java, then run rea doctor
REA won’t install Your Node.js is too old. Install the latest Node LTS
Android analysis fails Install the full Java JDK; the JRE isn’t enough
A tool asks for Python pwntools Only one tool needs it, so you can skip it
Saved report is missing results Run the analysis and the export in the same Claude Code session

Security tip: Only install REA from the official repo. Copycat repos are a common phishing trick.

If you remember one thing, make it rea doctor. It’s like a mechanic plugging a scanner into your car before touching anything: it changes nothing and tells you exactly what’s missing.

Verdict: Is REA Worth the Hype?

For understanding apps: yes. What used to take hours of clicking around tools like Ghidra took me minutes, explained in plain English. I learned more about VS Code’s internals in one session than I knew before.

But it’s not a magic clone button. Building something good with what you learn is still your job. Always check findings marked inferred or unknown before you trust them.

How I’ll Actually Use It

  1. Checking my own release builds: open my own APK and see what really ships, like leftover debug settings, keys or forgotten servers. A free security check before every release.
  2. Learning before building: study how a well-made open-source app implements a feature.
  3. Auditing the tools I install: see exactly which servers they talk to, like we did with VS Code.

REA won’t build an app for you in one click, but it gives your AI agent eyes inside any app, and it’s honest about what it doesn’t know.
